intro: Read the deck for the content and these notes for the thinking. Each note under a slide says what to remember, how to read the evidence and where evaluators slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself with the recall questions, and write your own notes in the space around mine.

sections.title: What Impact Evaluation Is
sections.big_idea: Impact evaluation answers one demanding question: **how much of the change did the programme cause**, compared with what would have happened anyway?
in_plain_words: An impact evaluation estimates the causal effect of a programme on an outcome. It needs a comparison group, measurement before and after, a stated identification strategy and a pre-specified outcome. Without those, a study can describe a change and cannot attribute it, which is a much weaker claim.

Monitoring asks whether you are on plan and can correct delivery. Impact evaluation asks whether the programme caused the change, and it is costly and slow. It sits alongside needs assessment, process evaluation and cost-effectiveness. **Use it where a real decision hangs on a causal question**, and commission it before the rollout design is fixed.

diagram.caption: monitoring on the left, impact evaluation on the right

key_terms.meaning: A study estimating a programme's causal effect on an outcome.
Routine tracking of inputs, activities and outputs against plan.
Showing the change was caused by the programme.
A check on whether the programme was delivered as designed.
The design argument that makes a comparison credible.

worked_example.title: Put each claim on the results chain
worked_example.setup: A programme report states: '1,200 toilets built' and 'diarrhoea fell in treated villages'.
steps: '1,200 toilets built' is an output, found on the monitoring side of the chain.
'Diarrhoea fell in treated villages' is an outcome, and attribution needs a counterfactual.
The report has no comparison group and no baseline, so it can describe the fall without attributing it.
The honest label is a report of outcomes, which says nothing about impact.
worked_example.answer: An output claim and an outcome claim; neither is an impact estimate without a comparison.

mistakes: Calling a before-and-after report an impact evaluation when it has no comparison group.
Claiming results at outcome level using output-level data.
Applying impact evaluation as a badge of rigour to programmes needing operational information.
Commissioning after the programme has already run everywhere.

recall.q: What four things does an impact evaluation require?
recall.a: A comparison group, measurement before and after, a stated identification strategy and a pre-specified outcome.

recall.q: Which of monitoring and impact evaluation can correct delivery?
recall.a: Monitoring; impact evaluation usually arrives too late.

recall.q: Where on the results chain does impact evaluation aim?
recall.a: At the far right: outcomes and impact.

recall.q: What question must always be asked of an improvement?
recall.a: Compared to what?

recall.q: When is an impact evaluation the wrong call?
recall.a: When the question is already established, nobody will act on it, the programme changes weekly or everyone is treated.

sections.title: The Counterfactual & Causal Inference
sections.big_idea: Impact is the outcome with the programme minus the outcome without it, and **the second half is never observed**, so every design builds a substitute.
in_plain_words: The counterfactual is what would have happened to the same people, in the same period, without the programme. A person cannot be treated and untreated at once, so causal inference is a missing-data problem, and evaluations estimate group averages. Before-after and participants-versus-non-participants comparisons fail because they confuse the programme with other changes or with who chose to join.

Selection bias arises from self-selection, placement, targeting and attrition. A good comparison group looks alike at baseline, shares outside forces and differs only in the programme. Estimands differ too: ATE, ATT and LATE answer different questions. **Every design makes one promise**: the comparison group stands in for the counterfactual.

diagram.note: every design is a way to estimate the missing term

key_terms.meaning: What would have happened to the same people without the programme.
Systematic differences between recipients and others that also affect outcomes.
Average effect if everyone in the population were treated.
Average effect among those who received the programme.
Effect on those an instrument moved.
A table showing groups look alike at baseline.

worked_example.title: Estimating impact with a substitute
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 62% of treated households have a toilet at endline. A credible comparison group suggests 48% would have had one without the programme.
steps: The observed outcome with the programme is 62%.
The counterfactual is unobservable, so use the comparison estimate of 48%.
Impact = 62 − 48 = 14 percentage points.
A before-after comparison would credit the programme with every other change as well.
worked_example.answer: About 14 percentage points, as long as the comparison group is a credible stand-in.

mistakes: Comparing completers with dropouts. It measures who could complete.
Assuming selection bias always overstates the effect. Targeting the worst-off understates it.
Quoting an ATT for a universal rollout decision, which needs the ATE.
Treating an evaluation as telling you what happened to any one participant.

recall.q: Define the counterfactual.
recall.a: What would have happened to the very same people, in the same period, had the programme not existed.

recall.q: Why is a before-after comparison a wrong counterfactual?
recall.a: It confuses the programme with everything else that changed over time.

recall.q: Name two sources of selection bias.
recall.a: Self-selection and programme placement, or administrative targeting or attrition.

recall.q: Which estimand does a scale-up decision need?
recall.a: The ATE.

recall.q: What does RD estimate?
recall.a: An effect local to the cutoff, valid for units near the threshold.

sections.title: Theory of Change & Evaluation Questions
sections.big_idea: A theory of change names the pathway and its assumptions, so that **a null result can be explained** and a sharp question can be written.
in_plain_words: A theory of change maps how activities lead to outcomes, link by link, with an assumption at each arrow. Without it you cannot choose outcomes, time the measurement or interpret a null. Programmes that fail usually fail at a checkable link, either in delivery or in the idea, and a process evaluation tells the two apart.

Turn the theory into questions on impact, mechanism, process, cost and heterogeneity, and write the impact question with its intervention, population, outcome, comparison and timeframe. Scope by the decision, and run an evaluability check before drawing up terms of reference. **If no answer would change the decision, do not run the evaluation.**

nodes.label: More spent on food and care

diagram.caption: each arrow is an assumption that can fail

key_terms.meaning: A map of how activities lead to outcomes, with assumptions.
The chain broke in delivery; the theory is untested.
Delivery worked; an assumed link did not.
Looking at for whom the programme worked.
A pre-commitment check that a programme can be evaluated credibly.

worked_example.title: Write the sharp question
worked_example.setup: Weak question: 'Does our programme help?' Rewrite using the five parts.
steps: Intervention: 18 months of monthly cash transfers.
Population: mothers of children under two.
Outcome: height-for-age z-score, measured at 24 months.
Comparison: versus no transfer, in comparable villages.
worked_example.answer: 'Does 18 months of monthly cash transfers to mothers of under-2s in Koraput reduce child stunting, relative to comparable villages without transfers?'

mistakes: Reading a null as 'the idea failed' when delivery may have broken.
Commissioning only the impact question and getting a number with no explanation.
Evaluating a programme that changes weekly.
Discovering an evaluability problem after an evaluator is contracted.

recall.q: What can you not do without a theory of change?
recall.a: Choose outcomes, interpret a null, time the measurement or test mechanisms.

recall.q: Which question types does a good evaluation answer?
recall.a: Impact, mechanism, process, cost and for whom.

recall.q: What are the five parts of a sharp question?
recall.a: Intervention, population, outcome, comparison and timeframe.

recall.q: What alternative applies when no comparison group is possible?
recall.a: Contribution analysis.

recall.q: Name two evaluability checks.
recall.a: A clear theory of change, measurable outcomes, a credible comparison, stable implementation or someone who will use the result.

sections.title: Randomised Experiments (RCTs)
sections.big_idea: A lottery builds the counterfactual: it balances what you can and cannot see, **provided** the randomisation survives the field.
in_plain_words: Random assignment makes groups comparable in expectation on observed and unobserved traits, so no other method has a stronger claim to internal validity. That holds over repeated trials and not in every sample, which is why you check the balance table, especially the baseline outcome.

Randomise individuals when treated and control people do not mix, and clusters when programmes work at group level or spillovers are likely. Clusters cost power, so you need many of them. Spillovers bias estimates, and ethics requires equipoise, with random phase-in as the standard answer. **Randomisation is easy to specify and hard to protect.**

key_terms.meaning: Units assigned to treatment or control by chance.
Real uncertainty about whether the programme works.
Everyone gets the programme; chance sets the order.
Treatment leaking to the control group.
A group assigned together, such as a village.
MIT-based lab running randomised evaluations.

worked_example.title: People and clusters
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a cluster design uses 40 villages of 50 people each.
steps: Total people: 40 × 50 = 2,000.
People per village: 2,000 ÷ 40 = 50.
An individually randomised study of 2,000 people has far more power.
The cluster design is weaker because power depends on the number of clusters as well as total people.
worked_example.answer: 2,000 people but only 40 clusters, so the cluster design is far weaker than 2,000 individually randomised people.

mistakes: Assuming randomisation guarantees a clean claim when compliance and attrition fail.
Skipping the balance table.
Randomising within a village for a village-level water scheme.
Withholding a known, effective, life-saving intervention to run a trial.

recall.q: What does randomisation balance that no other design can?
recall.a: Unobserved characteristics such as motivation and ability, in expectation.

recall.q: What is the first thing to check in any RCT?
recall.a: The baseline balance table.

recall.q: What is the standard example of positive spillover?
recall.a: Deworming: an untreated child benefits from treated neighbours.

recall.q: When is randomisation ethically defensible?
recall.a: When there is real uncertainty, resources cannot cover everyone, or a phase-in is used.

recall.q: Who shared the 2019 Nobel Prize for the experimental approach?
recall.a: Banerjee, Duflo and Kremer.

sections.title: Quasi-Experimental Designs
sections.big_idea: When you cannot randomise, exploit how allocation happened, and **name the assumption** each design needs.
in_plain_words: Difference-in-differences subtracts the comparison group's change from the treated group's change, and needs parallel trends, which cannot be tested directly. Regression discontinuity compares units just either side of a cutoff and gives a local effect. Matching builds a statistical twin from observed traits and cannot fix unobserved differences. Instrumental variables need relevance and the exclusion restriction.

Each design is only as credible as its assumption. Probe DiD with pre-period plots, RD with a density test and IV with argument and falsification tests. Matching cannot be tested at all. **If allocation was discretionary and undocumented, none of these applies**, and the honest answer is that the effect cannot be identified.

children.label: Difference-in-differences
items: Before and after, treated and comparison

diagram.caption: what each design exploits and assumes

key_terms.meaning: Change in the treated group minus change in the comparison group.
Groups would have moved together absent the programme.
Impact from the jump at an eligibility threshold.
Estimated probability of being treated, given characteristics.
The instrument affects the outcome only through take-up.

worked_example.title: A difference-in-differences estimate
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: treated group outcome 40 before and 60 after. Comparison group 38 before and 44 after.
steps: Treated change: 60 − 40 = 20.
Comparison change: 44 − 38 = 6.
Impact = 20 − 6 = 14.
This holds only if the groups would have moved in parallel without the programme.
worked_example.answer: An impact of 14 points, conditional on parallel trends.

mistakes: Reporting a DiD estimate with no pre-trend plot.
Describing a PSM estimate as causal without heavy caveats.
Generalising an RD effect to households far from the cutoff.
Using distance to a facility as an instrument without asking about other paths to the outcome.

recall.q: What does DiD remove?
recall.a: Fixed differences between groups and common time shocks.

recall.q: What is the main threat to RD?
recall.a: Manipulation of the score.

recall.q: What can matching never fix?
recall.a: Differences on unobserved variables.

recall.q: Name the two requirements of a valid instrument.
recall.a: Relevance and the exclusion restriction.

recall.q: Which design has no diagnostic?
recall.a: Matching; selection on observables cannot be tested.

sections.title: Choosing a Method
sections.big_idea: The best design is the most credible one that is **feasible and ethical** here, and execution matters as much as the rung on the ladder.
in_plain_words: Method choice trades off validity, feasibility, ethics and timeliness. Internal validity asks whether the answer is right for the people studied, and the credibility ladder runs from RCT down to before-after comparison. Feasibility is mostly timing: build the evaluation in before the programme starts, and use phased rollouts as natural comparison groups.

Mixed methods let you explain a number. A decision guide asks about random assignment, a cutoff, phased rollout with baseline and an external nudge, and the last answer, none of these, is often right. **A well-run simple design beats a botched fancy one**, so ask for the attrition rate by group first.

key_terms.meaning: Whether the study identifies the causal effect where it was run.
A ranking of designs by the quality of their counterfactual.
Staggered delivery that creates a comparison group.
Quantitative effect estimates with qualitative explanation.
A reasoned causal claim without a counterfactual estimate.

worked_example.title: Pick the design for each case
worked_example.setup: Use the decision guide on three situations.
steps: A district can be assigned at random and an ethics board approves: RCT.
Eligibility is a poverty score below a sharp cutoff: regression discontinuity.
Rollout is phased over three years with baseline data: DiD.
Everyone is treated at once with no baseline and no cutoff: reconsider the question and consider contribution analysis.
worked_example.answer: RCT, RD, DiD and, for the last case, no credible counterfactual design.

mistakes: Ranking designs from memory without asking what the assumption is.
Assuming a more rigorous design is always the better choice, whatever the execution.
Retrofitting an evaluation onto a finished programme.
Collecting qualitative accounts after the quantitative result is known.

recall.q: Which threat to internal validity is handled by no design?
recall.a: Differential attrition; only good execution controls it.

recall.q: What is the single biggest feasibility lever?
recall.a: Timing; build the design in before the programme starts.

recall.q: What does a phased rollout give you at no extra cost?
recall.a: A comparison group of those not yet reached.

recall.q: What do quantitative and qualitative work each answer?
recall.a: Quantitative: whether and how much. Qualitative: why and for whom.

recall.q: What should you ask for first when judging execution?
recall.a: The attrition rate by group.

sections.title: Sampling & Statistical Power
sections.big_idea: An underpowered study can bury a real effect, so **plan power before collecting data** and ask what the MDE is.
in_plain_words: Power is the probability of detecting a real effect of an assumed size, conventionally 80% or more. The minimum detectable effect asks the question the other way round: with this sample, what is the smallest impact we can see? If the MDE is larger than any plausible effect, the study cannot succeed.

Required sample rises with a smaller expected effect, more variability, a higher power target, clustering and attrition, and falls with a baseline. Clusters cost power through intra-cluster correlation, so add clusters as well as people. Type I and II errors carry different costs. **Insist on seeing the power calculation and the source of the assumed effect.**

diagram.caption: what pushes the sample up or down

key_terms.meaning: Probability of detecting a real effect of a given size.
Smallest true effect a study can reliably detect.
How alike people are within a cluster.
The factor by which clustering shrinks the effective sample.
Missing a real effect; risk is 1 − power.

worked_example.title: Halving the detectable effect
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 400 people per arm can detect a 10-point effect. You want to detect 5 points. Separately, a clustered sample of 2,000 has a design effect of 2.5.
steps: Halving the detectable effect roughly quadruples the sample.
Sample for 5 points: 400 × 4 = 1,600 per arm.
Effective clustered sample = n divided by the design effect.
2,000 ÷ 2.5 = 800 effective people.
worked_example.answer: About 1,600 per arm for the smaller effect, and an effective sample of 800 for the clustered design.

mistakes: Reading 'not significant' from an underpowered study as 'no effect'.
Assuming an effect size larger than any comparable programme achieved.
Counting total people for a cluster design instead of clusters.
Planning to the minimum sample with no allowance for attrition or partial take-up.

recall.q: What does 80% power mean?
recall.a: A real effect of the assumed size is detected four times in five.

recall.q: What does MDE stand for and mean?
recall.a: Minimum detectable effect: the smallest true effect the study can reliably detect.

recall.q: What halves the sample need or quadruples it?
recall.a: Halving the detectable effect roughly quadruples the required sample.

recall.q: What is Type I error?
recall.a: A false positive, controlled by the significance level, usually 5%.

recall.q: Which lever usually beats more respondents when budget is tight?
recall.a: Reducing outcome variance, for example with a baseline.

sections.title: Measurement & Data Collection
sections.big_idea: Fix outcomes and instruments **before** the study, and measure both groups the same way, or the measurement creates the result.
in_plain_words: Outcome indicators flow from the theory of change. Choose a primary outcome in advance, define it, and commit to the plan publicly through pre-registration. A usable indicator is valid, reliable, sensitive and feasible, and sensitivity most often defeats an evaluation. A baseline confirms balance and sharpens power.

Surveys fit the question exactly but cost more, while administrative data are cheap and cover everyone but may change when the programme changes. Social desirability, recall error, surveyor effects and differential measurement all bias results. Attrition and timing matter too. **Measure treatment and control groups identically, and blind enumerators where you can.**

diagram.caption: use both where you can; disagreement is informative

key_terms.meaning: The one or two outcomes on which success is judged.
Publicly recording hypotheses and plan before seeing data.
Measurement before the programme starts.
Loss of participants between baseline and endline.
Measuring the two groups differently.
Worst-case and best-case assumptions for those lost.

worked_example.title: Attrition by arm
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 1,000 households per arm at baseline. At endline 850 treatment and 950 control households are found.
steps: Treatment lost: 1,000 − 850 = 150.
Treatment attrition: 150 ÷ 1,000 = 15%.
Control lost: 1,000 − 950 = 50.
Control attrition: 50 ÷ 1,000 = 5%.
worked_example.answer: Attrition is 15% against 5%, so it differs by arm and needs testing and bounding.

mistakes: Choosing the outcome that moved after the data arrive.
Using an outcome that cannot move within the study period.
Improving the survey instrument between baseline and endline.
Treating a declaration or administrative figure as outcome data without checking how records changed.

recall.q: What are the four properties of a usable indicator?
recall.a: Valid, reliable, sensitive and feasible.

recall.q: What does a baseline give you?
recall.a: Balance verification, variance reduction, heterogeneity by baseline status and a DiD fallback.

recall.q: Which bias is the most dangerous for an impact estimate?
recall.a: Differential measurement between treatment and control.

recall.q: What is the standard response to attrition?
recall.a: Bounding exercises, reporting the rate by arm and testing balance.

recall.q: What should set the timing of the endline?
recall.a: The theory of change: when the outcome should plausibly respond.

sections.title: Analysis & Interpreting Results
sections.big_idea: Read effect size and uncertainty together, because **significance is not importance** and a null can be real or empty.
in_plain_words: Report the effect in units a decision-maker understands and add the standardised size for comparison. Statistical significance speaks to confidence only. The confidence interval gives four readings: firm and useful, firm but trivial, narrow and small, or wide and uninformative. A wide interval including zero is an underpowered study.

ITT is the effect of being offered a programme and ToT the effect on those who took it up. Heterogeneity analysis needs pre-specified subgroups. Test twenty outcomes and about one will look significant by chance. **Check implementation before concluding anything from a null**, because a programme that was not delivered has not been tested.

children.label: Interval excludes zero
items: All values trivial: real yet small

children.label: Interval includes zero
items: Narrow: probably a small true effect

key_terms.meaning: How much the outcome changed, in units a decision-maker understands.
The range of plausible effects; its width shows precision.
Effect of being offered the programme, by original assignment.
Effect on those who actually took up the programme.
Reporting only the outcomes that look significant.
A well-powered study with a tight interval around zero.

worked_example.title: Read an interval and count false alarms
worked_example.setup: A study reports 6 percentage points with a confidence interval of 2 to 10. A useful effect is 3 points. A second study tests 20 independent outcomes at the usual 5% threshold.
steps: The interval excludes zero, so the effect is reasonably firm.
It includes values above 3, so a useful effect is plausible.
Expected false positives in the second study: 20 × 5 ÷ 100 = 1.
So one 'significant' outcome out of 20 is what chance alone would give.
worked_example.answer: The first study shows reasonable evidence of a worthwhile impact. The second is expected to produce one false alarm.

mistakes: Reading the p-value alone.
Quoting the ToT without the take-up rate.
Treating a surprising subgroup result as a conclusion.
Reporting an inconclusive study as a null.

recall.q: What does a wide interval that includes zero mean?
recall.a: The study is uninformative, probably underpowered.

recall.q: Which estimate is usually policy-relevant, ITT or ToT?
recall.a: ITT, because governments offer and face incomplete take-up.

recall.q: How many false positives do twenty independent tests give by chance?
recall.a: About one at the usual threshold.

recall.q: Name two features of a real null.
recall.a: Well-powered with a tight interval around zero; implementation verified; take-up adequate.

recall.q: Which question catches the most problems in a report?
recall.a: Whether the primary outcome is the pre-specified one.

sections.title: External Validity, Cost & Ethics
sections.big_idea: A result must travel, be worth its **cost per rupee**, and be produced ethically and transparently.
in_plain_words: External validity asks whether a result holds elsewhere. It breaks on context, implementation quality, scale effects and population. Mechanism travels better than a headline number. Cost-effectiveness asks how much outcome you buy per rupee, using costs at scale, and a smaller effect that costs a tenth as much may be the better buy.

Ethics covers consent, do no harm, privacy and independent review, and refusing the study should not affect access to the programme. Pre-registration prevents cherry-picking, and the file-drawer problem means the published record overstates what works. **Trust systematic reviews and registries over a single splashy study.**

key_terms.meaning: Whether a result holds in another place, time or population.
Changes that appear once everyone is treated.
Outcome bought per rupee.
Independent review board approving the design.
Null results left unpublished.
A synthesis across studies that corrects publication bias.

worked_example.title: Impact per rupee
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: programme A raises an outcome by 6 points at Rs 600 per child. Programme B raises it by 5 points at Rs 60 per child.
steps: Cost per point for A: 600 ÷ 6 = 100 rupees.
Cost per point for B: 60 ÷ 5 = 12 rupees.
B costs a tenth of A per child: 60 ÷ 600 = 0.1.
B's smaller effect is still the better buy, if the costs are at scale.
worked_example.answer: A costs Rs 100 per point and B Rs 12 per point, so B is the better buy.

mistakes: Treating a clean result from one district as a general finding.
Using pilot costs for a scale-up decision.
Letting refusal of the research cost a person access to the programme.
Relying on one published study without asking whether a review exists.

recall.q: What four things break transfer?
recall.a: Context, implementation quality, scale effects and population.

recall.q: What does cost-effectiveness require?
recall.a: A common outcome unit and full cost data, at scale for scale-up decisions.

recall.q: What is pre-registration?
recall.a: Publicly recording hypotheses, primary outcome and analysis plan before seeing the data.

recall.q: Which registries are named?
recall.a: The AEA RCT Registry and 3ie's records.

recall.q: What is the file-drawer problem?
recall.a: Null results often go unpublished, so the record overstates what works.

sections.title: Using IE for Decisions & Further Reading
sections.big_idea: Commission early, ask five hard questions of any proposal, and **agree who will act** on whatever the evidence says.
in_plain_words: Your influence as commissioner is greatest before the contract is signed. Define the decision, write a sharp question, bring the evaluator in at design stage, demand a power calculation and identification strategy, and require pre-registration. In a proposal meeting, ask for the counterfactual, the assumption, the MDE, the handling of attrition and spillovers, and the plan for pre-registration.

Impact evaluation reports on a specific programme in a specific place, and cannot say what to value. Evidence goes unused when it arrives late, is framed for academics, has no owner or is shelved. Further reading starts with Gertler and colleagues. **Name an owner at commissioning** and settle publication terms before any result exists.

key_terms.meaning: The person who frames the question and judges the design.
The brief for the evaluator, written after evaluability.
A 3ie tool showing what has and has not been studied.
A non-academic summary of the finding.
A synthesis of studies; check before commissioning.

worked_example.title: Test a proposal's assumed effect
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a proposal assumes a 10-point effect. The best comparable programmes achieved 4 points.
steps: Ask what effect was assumed and where it came from.
Compare: 10 − 4 = 6 points above the best comparable result.
Ratio: 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 times the comparable effect.
The slide calls this the commonest failure: a comfortable and useless sample.
worked_example.answer: The assumed effect is 6 points, or 2.5 times, above any comparable result, so the power calculation is unreliable.

mistakes: Asking questions only when the report lands, after your influence has gone.
Disqualifying a proposal for a weak answer instead of using it to start the design conversation.
Treating an effect size as a decision.
Skipping a search for a systematic review that already answers the question.

recall.q: When is a commissioner's influence greatest?
recall.a: Before the contract is signed.

recall.q: What five questions should you ask an evaluator?
recall.a: The counterfactual, what must be true to identify the effect, the MDE, attrition and spillovers handling, and pre-registration.

recall.q: What can impact evaluation not tell you?
recall.a: What to value, how to weigh trade-offs, or whether the result will hold at scale.

recall.q: Who wrote Impact Evaluation in Practice?
recall.a: Gertler, Martinez, Premand, Rawlings and Vermeersch.

recall.q: What is the cheapest possible evaluation?
recall.a: Checking whether a systematic review already answers your question.

notes.2: Use the agenda to see the deck as one argument in eleven steps: the question, the counterfactual, the theory, then designs, choice, sample, measurement, analysis, validity and use. If you commission evaluations instead of running them, give extra time to sections 6, 7 and 11. Those are where a commissioner's choices matter most.
notes.4: Hold onto the four requirements: a comparison group, measurement before and after, a stated identification strategy and a pre-specified outcome. **If any one is missing, the study can describe a change and cannot attribute it.** Such reports are still worth reading, as long as you describe them as reports of outcomes.
notes.5: Monitoring asks whether you are on plan, and impact evaluation asks whether you caused the change. The last row of the second table is the one to remember: **monitoring is the only one of the two that can change delivery while the programme runs.** You need both, because they answer different questions.
notes.6: Place each claim on the chain: inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, impact. Monitoring sits on the left and impact evaluation on the far right. The commonest reporting error is on the slide: **claiming results at outcome level using data from the output level**. Ask which link your evidence actually measures.
notes.7: Whenever a village improves, ask 'compared to what?'. A good monsoon, rising incomes or another scheme could explain it. The last row on the slide is the one under your control: **programmes are placed where they are likely to succeed**, which is selection bias, and it is excluded by design and not by argument.
notes.8: Read the two columns as costs and benefits of evidence. With it you scale what works, stop what does not and learn the mechanism. The second row saves the most money and is hardest institutionally, because stopping a programme has an identifiable loser. **That is a political problem that rigour alone cannot solve.**
notes.9: This slide is a brake. Impact evaluation is costly and slow, and good monitoring and process evaluation serve you better much of the time. Use the left column as a test of five conditions: open causal question, a real decision, a stable programme, a credible comparison and a budget. **Knowing when not to commission is half the course.**
notes.10: Most readers will commission instead of estimating, and that still takes literacy: framing the question, judging a design, reading a power calculation and telling a null from an inconclusive result. The single most valuable act is on the slide: **bring the evaluator in before the rollout design is fixed**.
notes.11: Place impact evaluation among its cousins by the question each answers. The timing table carries the practical lesson: an impact evaluation is executed afterwards but **must be designed before the programme starts**. Pair it with process evaluation so a null can be traced to the idea or to delivery.
notes.13: Memorise the definition of impact: the outcome with the programme minus the outcome without it, for the same group. We observe the first and never the second. **When reading any evaluation, find the sentence that states the counterfactual.** If there is none, there is no impact estimate.
notes.14: Think of causal inference as a missing-data problem. One person cannot be treated and untreated at once, so the individual effect stays unseen and we estimate group averages instead. A consequence worth stating to funders: **an evaluation tells you about an average and says nothing about what happened to any one participant**.
notes.15: Check each of the four wrong counterfactuals against programme reports you know: before-after, participants against non-participants, treated villages against a national average, completers against dropouts. The slide says all four are cheap and wrong. The fourth is the most seductive, since it **measures persistence and says nothing about the training**.
notes.16: Selection bias mixes the programme's effect with pre-existing differences. Four sources are listed: self-selection, placement, administrative targeting and attrition. The third row points the other way, since targeting the worst-off makes a naive comparison understate the effect. **Knowing the direction tells you whether your estimate is an upper or lower bound.**
notes.17: The illustrative chart shows volunteers who differ before the programme starts. The key idea sits in the right-hand column: motivation and prior education drive both joining and later results. **That is what makes it selection bias and not mere difference.** A comparison of joiners and non-joiners measures who joined.
notes.18: Use the three conditions as a checklist for any comparison group: alike at baseline, exposed to the same outside forces, and different only in the programme. The last row is checked least. **Ask the evaluator what else was happening in the comparison area**, because a village receiving a different scheme is no counterfactual for yours.
notes.19: Always ask which estimand a study reports, and which your decision needs. ATE is the effect if everyone were treated, ATT the effect on those actually treated, and LATE the effect on those an instrument moved. **A scale-up decision needs the ATE.** Regression discontinuity adds a fourth case, an effect local to the cutoff.
notes.20: Every design makes one promise: my comparison group stands in for the treatment group's counterfactual. The RCT promises chance, RD the cutoff, DiD a shared trend, matching observed traits and IV an instrument with one path. **Ask any evaluator to state the assumption in one sentence**; if they cannot, the design is not identified.
notes.22: Without a stated chain of cause and effect you cannot choose outcomes, time the measurement or test mechanisms. The sharpest consequence is on the slide: **a null result without a theory of change is uninterpretable**. It says the outcome did not move and nothing about why.
notes.23: Trace the chain link by link: transfer, income, food spending, nutrition, stunting. Each arrow is an assumption that can fail independently. **Measure intermediate outcomes**, because that turns the evaluation into a diagnosis and not a verdict, and the cost is small once you are already collecting data.
notes.24: Separate implementation failure from theory failure. In the first, the chain was never delivered and the theory is untested. In the second, delivery worked and an assumed link did not. A process evaluation alongside the impact evaluation tells them apart, so you do not **abandon a good idea or persist with a bad one**.
notes.25: Match each type of question to the method that answers it: impact, mechanism, process, cost and heterogeneity. Commissioning only the first leaves you with a number and no explanation. The slide suggests bundling at least the first three, and the cost question is **the cheapest addition**, as costing data usually exists.
notes.26: Write your question with five parts: intervention, population, outcome, comparison and timeframe. The strong example names 18 months of monthly transfers to mothers of under-2s in Koraput, with stunting as the outcome. **If your question cannot be written this way, it is not yet a question.**
notes.27: Let the decision dictate the question. Ask what you would do differently if the answer were yes or no. If nothing changes, skip the evaluation. The most useful question is the last: **what answer would change the decision?**, since it converts vague interest in impact into a specific minimum detectable effect.
notes.28: Learn the five reasons to decline: a programme changing weekly, an operational question, no possible comparison group, no budget for rigour and a decision already made. The slide offers an alternative for each, such as process evaluation or contribution analysis. **A weak impact evaluation is worse than none.**
notes.29: Run an evaluability check before writing the terms of reference. The five tests are a clear theory of change, measurable outcomes, a credible comparison, stable implementation and someone who will use the result. The slide notes it costs a few days and can **save an entire evaluation budget**.
notes.31: A lottery makes the two groups comparable in expectation. The right-hand column lists the provisos where field RCTs actually fail: enough units, real randomisation, compliance with no spillover, and low attrition. **Randomisation is easy to specify and hard to protect.** In a single trial groups can still differ by chance, so check balance.
notes.32: Randomisation balances what you can see and what you cannot, such as motivation, ability and family support, in expectation. That unique claim gives a well-run RCT the strongest internal validity. Note the qualifier on the slide: **it holds over repeated trials and not in any one sample**, so sample size and balance checks still matter.
notes.33: Read the baseline balance table first in any RCT. If randomisation worked, the groups look alike on every measured characteristic. A few differences are expected, but **imbalance on the baseline outcome itself should give you pause**. A paper without a balance table withholds the first thing a reader should see.
notes.34: J-PAL, based at MIT, champions randomised evaluations of anti-poverty programmes, and 3ie funds and synthesises evidence across the Global South. The 2019 Nobel Prize went to Banerjee, Duflo and Kremer for the experimental approach. The practical use: **J-PAL's evidence reviews are a useful first stop** before commissioning anything.
notes.35: The chart is schematic, and the message is the direction: randomised evaluation went from rare to mainstream. The critique in the right column is that questions were chosen for tractability and external validity is weak. **Hold both readings**: the method is strongest for the questions it fits and fits only some.
notes.36: Choose the unit by the intervention. Individual assignment is more efficient but risky if people mix. Cluster assignment suits village-level programmes but needs many clusters. The slide's example: **40 villages of 50 people is far weaker than 2,000 individually randomised people**, because power depends on the number of clusters.
notes.37: Spillover means treatment leaks to controls, as when a dewormed child stops infecting a neighbour. Positive spillover understates the impact and negative spillover overstates it. The defences listed are randomising at a higher level, buffer areas, or **measuring the spillover as its own estimate**.
notes.38: Equipoise is the ethical condition: real uncertainty about whether the programme works. Random phase-in resolves most of the objection, since everyone eventually receives it and only the order is random. **Where the intervention is already established, withholding it for a study is not defensible.** Independent review adds a safeguard.
notes.40: When you cannot randomise, ask first how people came to be treated, because each design exploits a feature of the allocation. A past programme suggests DiD, a cutoff suggests RD, a phased rollout suggests DiD and an external nudge suggests IV. **If allocation was discretionary and undocumented, none applies.**
notes.41: DiD takes the change in the treated group minus the change in the comparison group. That removes fixed group differences and common time shocks, but **does not remove differential trends or shocks that hit one group only**. Say the formula aloud: treated change minus comparison change.
notes.42: In the illustrative chart, the dashed line is the assumed counterfactual, and the gap above it (about 14 points) is the estimated impact. The counterfactual is drawn like data but is an assumption. **Several pre-periods are much stronger evidence than one**, since a single pre-period cannot show a trend at all.
notes.43: Parallel trends means the groups would have moved together without the programme. If they were already diverging, DiD credits the programme with the divergence. The assumption concerns the unobserved period, so it cannot be tested directly. **Ask for the pre-trend plot**: without one the key assumption has not been examined.
notes.44: RD compares units just above and just below an eligibility line, such as a poverty score of 0.33. They are nearly alike apart from the programme. The limits: it gives only a local effect, and **manipulation of the score is the main threat**. Check you have enough observations near the cutoff.
notes.45: Read the jump at the cutoff (about 14 points in the illustration) as the estimated effect. RD is credible and visual, but local. For a scale-up decision covering everyone eligible, **it is not the estimate you need**, and saying so is part of reading it accurately. It gives no protection if the score is manipulated.
notes.46: Matching builds a statistical twin from observed characteristics, and PSM matches on one number, the estimated probability of treatment. Its fatal limit is on the slide: **matching can only balance what you measured**. Motivation or hidden need stays unbalanced, so describing a PSM estimate as causal without caveats overstates it.
notes.47: An instrument must do two things: predict take-up, which is testable, and affect the outcome only through take-up, the exclusion restriction, which can only be argued. Distance to a facility is common and contested because **distance may affect outcomes through other paths**, such as access to markets.
notes.48: Use the second table as your question list: DiD is probed with pre-period plots, RD with a density test at the cutoff, matching cannot be tested, and IV is argued with falsification tests. **Three of four have a partial diagnostic**, and the one without any is the one most often used. Ask for the diagnostic.
notes.50: There is no single best method. Validity, feasibility, ethics and timeliness pull in different directions, and the best design is the most credible one that is feasible and ethical for you. **State the trade-off you made in the report.** Pretending there was none is the mark of a less serious evaluation.
notes.51: Internal validity asks whether the answer is right for the people and place studied. The table pairs each threat with a design, and the last row stands out: **differential attrition is handled by no design, only by good execution**, since it arises after assignment. A strong design is not a guarantee about the study.
notes.52: Read the ladder from RCT at the top down to naive comparison at the bottom, then read the third column of the second table, which names each design's weak point. The ranking is about the identifying assumption and not statistical sophistication. **A credible quasi-experiment beats a badly run RCT.**
notes.53: Before writing terms of reference, answer four feasibility questions: is there a stage left to assign or compare, do baseline data exist, is the sample large enough, and will the result arrive in time? The biggest lever is timing, so **design the evaluation in before the programme starts** and not afterwards.
notes.54: A phased rollout is a gift to evaluators. The areas not yet reached form a comparison group at no extra cost, the order can be randomised, and everyone eventually receives the programme. The slide's demand on commissioners is small: **someone must be asked before the phasing order is fixed**, because afterwards the opportunity is gone.
notes.55: Quantitative work answers whether it worked and by how much, and qualitative work explains why and for whom. The strongest evaluations combine both. A practical rule from the slide: **collect the qualitative material before the result is known**, or the accounts become explanations for a conclusion already in hand.
notes.56: Walk the five questions in order: assign at random, sharp cutoff, phased rollout with baseline, external nudge, then none of these. The last row is a real option and often the right answer. Where none applies, **contribution analysis and process tracing** give an evidenced causal claim without a counterfactual estimate; say which you are doing.
notes.57: Execution decides everything in the field. High attrition, differential attrition, spillovers, non-compliance and broken randomisation can each leave an RCT weaker than a careful quasi-experiment. The one check to run first: **ask for the attrition rate by group**, as it shows whether the design survived contact with the field.
notes.59: An underpowered study can miss a real, useful effect and tempt you to conclude 'no impact'. The slide separates a precise zero from an imprecise nothing, the single most misread thing in evaluation reporting. **Report the confidence interval, always**, because a point estimate cannot tell the two apart.
notes.60: Eighty per cent power means a real effect of the assumed size is found four times in five and missed once in five. The convention is a norm and not a law, and for a high-stakes decision higher power may be worth the cost. **If the true effect is smaller than assumed, the study is less powered than it says.**
notes.61: Turn the sample-size question around: with this sample, what is the smallest effect we can see? If your MDE is a 10-point gain and the programme can deliver 3, the study fails before it starts. **Ask for the MDE in the outcome's units** and compare it with what would matter.
notes.62: Effect size is the headline driver of sample size: halving the detectable effect roughly quadruples the sample. Variability, a higher power target, clustering and expected attrition all raise the required sample. A baseline measurement is the lever that saves money, since it **reduces the variance to be explained**.
notes.63: The illustrative curve rises steeply, then flattens as it nears 1, with 80% reached at about 1,000 per arm. Doubling a small sample buys a lot and doubling a large one buys little. Where budget is tight, the better lever is usually **reducing outcome variance**, such as a baseline or a better instrument.
notes.64: Clusters cost power because people within a village resemble each other and carry less independent information. Intra-cluster correlation and the design effect measure the loss. The practical rule: **more clusters buys more power than more people per cluster**, so forty large villages can be weaker than a hundred small ones.
notes.65: Follow the five steps: state the MDE, estimate variability, account for clustering, attrition and partial take-up, then solve for 80% power. The commonest failure is **assuming an effect size larger than any comparable programme achieved**, which produces a comfortable and useless sample. Ask what effect was assumed and where it came from.
notes.66: Type I error is a false positive, controlled by the 5% significance level, and Type II error is a false negative, controlled by power. The asymmetry in the last row is a real problem: **the false-negative risk is set four times higher by convention** and is rarely discussed. For costly abandonment, reconsider the balance.
notes.68: Choose outcomes from the theory of change before the evaluation starts, define them precisely and commit. Pre-registration makes the commitment visible and separates a test from a search. It also protects the evaluator: **a pre-specified null is defensible**, while a null after twenty specifications invites the question of what else was tried.
notes.69: Test your primary indicator against four properties: valid, reliable, sensitive and feasible. Sensitivity most often defeats an evaluation. **Check that the primary outcome could move by more than the MDE within the study period.** An outcome that cannot move in eighteen months guarantees a null.
notes.70: A baseline does double duty: it confirms balance and sharpens power by letting you control for starting levels. It also offers heterogeneity analysis and **a fallback if randomisation fails**, in the form of a DiD option. Skip it only if you must. A subsample baseline can deliver much of the variance reduction cheaply.
notes.71: Compare survey and administrative data by fit, cost, coverage, error type and risk. Surveys fit exactly but cost more and suffer recall error. The risk specific to administrative data is the last row: **if the programme changes how records are kept, the measure moves without the outcome moving**. Using both is strongest.
notes.72: Four biases can corrupt a finding quietly. The most dangerous for impact is differential measurement: if treated respondents are surveyed more enthusiastically, **you manufacture an effect out of thin air**. Measure both groups identically, and try to blind enumerators to treatment status, especially for observed or scored outcomes.
notes.73: Pilot every instrument, use neutral wording, blind enumerators where possible and keep the same instrument and timing for both groups. The last row is violated routinely and with good intentions: **improving the tool between baseline and endline destroys the comparison**. If the tool must change, run both at the changeover.
notes.74: Attrition is dangerous when high, when it differs between arms, or when it relates to the outcome. Track it, report it by arm and examine the baseline characteristics of leavers. Because it arises after randomisation, **no design protects against it**. Bounding exercises give the worst and best cases, and their width shows how much it mattered.
notes.75: Let the theory of change set the clock. Measure too early and the effect has not appeared, and measure too late and it may have faded. A stunting claim at six months has not allowed the mechanism to operate. **Two follow-ups beat one**, since they separate a delayed effect from a fading one.
notes.77: Report the effect in units a decision-maker understands: percentage points, rupees per household, days of schooling. Add the standardised size for comparison across studies. The slide's rule costs one extra column: **give the natural unit for the decision and the standardised size for comparability**.
notes.78: Statistical significance speaks to confidence and says nothing about size or importance. A huge sample can make a trivial effect significant, and a small sample can hide a large one. **Ask what effect would justify the cost, then check whether the confidence interval includes it.** Never read the p-value alone.
notes.79: Read the interval as well as the stars. An interval excluding zero with useful values is reasonable evidence, one excluding zero with trivial values is real but not worth it, a narrow one including zero suggests a small effect, and a wide one including zero is uninformative. **The bottom two rows separate a real null from an inconclusive study.**
notes.80: ITT compares everyone assigned to treatment, whether or not they took it up, and ToT looks at those who did. ITT reflects real rollout and is usually the policy-relevant number. ToT is larger. **A report quoting ToT without the take-up rate gives the flattering number without its context.** Keep groups by original assignment.
notes.81: Averages can hide wide variation, so look for differences by sex, caste, wealth or region. Pre-specify the subgroups, because with enough subgroups one will look significant by chance. Subgroup samples are also smaller by construction. **Treat surprising findings as hypotheses for next time** and never as conclusions.
notes.82: A null result is knowledge, if you can tell a real null from an empty one. A real null has a well-powered study and a tight interval around zero, with implementation verified. An empty null has a wide interval. **Check implementation before concluding anything**: a programme that was not delivered has not been tested.
notes.83: Use the five questions on any evaluation report: identification, balance, attrition, outcomes and take-up. The fourth catches the most: **a switched primary outcome is common and rarely flagged in a summary**. These checks identify most of the problems a specialist reviewer would find.
notes.84: With twenty independent outcomes at the usual threshold, about one will appear significant even when the programme does nothing. Defences are a pre-specified primary outcome, a limited number of tests and adjustment for multiple comparisons. The commissioner's rule: **insist on one pre-specified primary outcome** and treat everything else as exploratory.
notes.86: Keep internal and external validity apart. Internal validity asks whether the answer is right here, and external validity asks whether it transfers. The second is built by replication and understanding the mechanism. **A well-identified result from one district is not a general finding**, however clean the design.
notes.87: Four things break transfer: context, implementation, scale effects and population. The second row is the most common and least discussed, since a research-team pilot with intensive supervision is not what a government will deliver. **Ask why it worked and whether those conditions exist where you want to use it**: mechanism travels better.
notes.88: Pair every effect size with a credible cost figure, because the question is impact per rupee. A smaller-impact programme costing a tenth as much may be the better buy. **Collect cost data during the evaluation**, and use costs at scale and not pilot costs for scale-up decisions.
notes.89: Ethics covers both the programme and the study: informed consent, do no harm, privacy and independent review. The first row carries a distinction worth stating: **refusing to take part in the research should not affect access to the programme**. Also weigh the survey burden on populations already surveyed often.
notes.90: Pre-registration records the hypothesis, primary outcome, analysis plan and subgroups before you see the data, and registries such as the AEA RCT Registry make the plan public and time-stamped. For a commissioner the action is cheap: **require pre-registration in the terms of reference**, which substantially raises the credibility of what comes back.
notes.91: The published record overstates what works, because big, positive and novel results are published and nulls are shelved. So prefer systematic reviews and registries to a single splashy study. **Check whether a review searched for unpublished work.** 3ie and the Campbell Collaboration synthesise across studies to correct this bias.
notes.93: Follow the five steps in order: define the decision, write a sharp question, bring in the evaluator, demand a power calculation and identification strategy, then commit to a pre-registered plan. Your influence is greatest before the contract is signed. **Bringing the evaluator in early determines whether the rest is possible**, as the slide says.
notes.94: Take these five questions into any proposal meeting: counterfactual, identifying assumption, MDE, handling of attrition and spillovers, and pre-registration. None needs technical training. A weak answer need not disqualify a proposal; it marks **the conversation to have before the design is fixed**, and not after.
notes.95: Impact evaluation reports whether a specific programme worked in a specific place. It cannot say what to value, how to weigh trade-offs or whether the result will hold at scale. **The number is an input to a decision, never the decision itself.** A null concerns this version of the programme and not the idea.
notes.96: Four reasons evidence goes unused are late findings, academic framing, no owner for follow-through and shelved nulls. Each has a fix, such as aligning the timeline to the decision or commissioning a practitioner brief. **Name an owner at commissioning**, and settle publication terms in the contract before any result exists.
notes.97: Gertler and colleagues' Impact Evaluation in Practice, from the World Bank, is the free standard handbook and the natural next step. It covers counterfactuals, every design in this deck, power calculation and commissioning. **Read the design chapters and the power chapter first**: they carry most of what a commissioner needs.
notes.98: Use the table as a directory: J-PAL for randomised evaluations and training, 3ie for impact evaluations and reviews of the Global South, Campbell for systematic reviews, the AEA RCT Registry for checking pre-registration, and DIME for methods. **Before commissioning anything, check whether a systematic review already answers your question.**
notes.99: Carry five questions into every report or proposal: what is the counterfactual, was assignment random, what is the assumption and does it hold, what is the MDE, and what does the interval include? **If you carry one, carry the first**: most weak impact claims fail on it immediately.
